rfc970.title: On Packet Switches With Infinite Storage
rfc970.author: John Nagle
rfc970.venue: Network Working Group, Request for Comments: 970, FACC Palo Alto
rfc970.quote: We demonstrate the unexpected result that a datagram network with infinite storage, first-in-first-out queuing, at least two packet switches, and a finite packet lifetime will, under overload, drop all packets.
rfc970.quote2: The queue length for the outgoing link will then grow until the transit time through the queue exceeds the time-to-live of the incoming packets.
rfc970.quote3: if the departure rate is greater than one per time-to-live unit, the time-to-live of any forwarded packet will be exactly one.
rfc970.quote4: This is a rather unexpected result.  But it is quite real.  It is not an artifact of the infinite-buffer assumption.  The problem still occurs in networks with finite storage, but the effects are less clearly seen.
rfc970.quote5: But collectively, as the hosts overload the network, total throughput drops.  As shown above, throughput may drop to zero.
supports: December 1985 date on the RFC header line
infinite storage + FIFO + finite packet lifetime => drops all packets under overload
the queue grows until transit time exceeds TTL; forwarded packets carry TTL 1 and the next hop zeroes them
RFC 970 is not argument-only: Nagle reports an experiment (supermini as switch, 916 datagrams queued at peak)
front matter: Network Working Group, John Nagle, FACC Palo Alto, December 1985; 9 pages
rfc970.quote6: This problem is not just theoretical.  We have demonstrated it experimentally on our own network, using a supermini with several megabytes of memory as a switch.
rfc970.quote7: Our first experiment, using an Ethernet on one side of the switch and a 9600 baud line on the other, resulted in 916 IP datagrams queued in the switch at peak.

rfc896.title: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks
rfc896.author: John Nagle
rfc896.venue: Network Working Group, Request For Comments: 896, Ford Aerospace and Communications Corporation
rfc896.quote: In this condition every packet is being transmitted several times and throughput is reduced to a small fraction of normal.
rfc896.quote2: IP gateways are vulnerable to a phenomenon we call "congestion collapse", especially when such gateways connect networks of widely different bandwidth.
rfc896.quote3: This condition is stable.  Once the saturation point has been reached, if the algorithm for selecting packets to be dropped is fair, the network will continue to operate in a degraded condition.
rfc896.quote4: We have pushed our network into this condition experimentally and observed its stability.
rfc896.quote5: Hosts are sending each packet several times, and eventually some copy of each packet arrives at its destination.  This is congestion collapse.
supports: the term 'congestion collapse' is coined here, dated 6 January 1984
the collapsed state is stable, not a spike
Nagle's affiliation: Ford Aerospace and Communications Corporation
Nagle wrote it from Ford Aerospace, which ran what the memo calls the only private IP/TCP long-haul network in existence at the time
the memo's two named problems are the small-packet problem and the source-quench problem
an IMP is an ARPANET switching node
rfc896.quote6: Ford Aerospace and Communications Corporation, and its parent company, Ford Motor Company, operate the only private IP/TCP long-haul network in existence today.
rfc896.quote7: Two key problems with the engineering of TCP implementations have been observed; we call these the small-packet problem and the source-quench problem.
rfc896.quote8: ARPANET IMP based networks traditionally have uniform bandwidth and identical switching nodes, and are sized with substantial excess capacity.

jacobson1988.title: Congestion Avoidance and Control
jacobson1988.author: Van Jacobson, Michael J. Karels
jacobson1988.venue: Revised version (November 1988) of the paper presented at ACM SIGCOMM '88, Stanford, CA, August 1988
jacobson1988.quote: In October of '86, the Internet had the first of what became a series of 'congestion collapses'. During this period, the data throughput from LBL to UC Berkeley (sites separated by 400 yards and two IMP hops) dropped from 32 Kbps to 40 bps.
jacobson1988.quote2: We were fascinated by this sudden factor-of-thousand drop in bandwidth and embarked on an investigation of why things had gotten so bad.
jacobson1988.quote3: Since that time, we have put seven new algorithms into the 4BSD TCP:
jacobson1988.quote4: The phrase congestion collapse (describing a positive feedback instability due to poor retransmit timers) is again the coinage of John Nagle, this time from [23].
jacobson1988.note: Venue guard: the PDF's own footnote reads 'Note: This is a very slightly revised version of a paper originally presented at SIGCOMM '88 [12]. If you wish to reference this work, please cite [12].' Reference [12] in the same PDF is 'JACOBSON, V. Congestion avoidance and control. In Proceedings of SIGCOMM '88 (Stanford, CA, Aug. 1988), ACM.' -- the proceedings entry names Jacobson alone; the revised PDF read here carries both Jacobson (LBL) and Karels (UC Berkeley) on the byline and is dated November, 1988. Numbers quoted above are from the PDF, not from an index or an abstract page.
supports: 32 Kbps to 40 bps between LBL and UC Berkeley, 400 yards and two IMP hops apart
the fixes went into the 4BSD TCP as seven new algorithms

rfc6633.title: Deprecation of ICMP Source Quench Messages
rfc6633.author: F. Gont
rfc6633.venue: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), Request for Comments: 6633, Standards Track; Updates 792, 1122, 1812
rfc6633.quote: This document formally deprecates the use of ICMP Source Quench messages by transport protocols, formally updating RFC 792, RFC 1122, and RFC 1812.
rfc6633.quote2: ICMP Source Quench has been known to be an ineffective (and unfair) antidote for congestion, and generation of ICMP Source Quench messages by routers has been formally deprecated by [RFC1812] since 1995.
rfc6633.quote3: Widespread deployment of ICMP filtering makes it impossible to rely on ICMP Source Quench messages for congestion control.
supports: the explicit 'slow down' message was deprecated in May 2012
router generation of it had already been deprecated since 1995
the surviving congestion signal is loss, not a message
Source Quench described as 'an ineffective (and unfair) antidote for congestion'
rfc6633.quote4: Virtually all popular host implementations have removed support for ICMP Source Quench messages since (at least) 2005 [RFC5927].

unverified: Any currency figure for the October 1986 collapse. Neither Jacobson & Karels nor either RFC prices the outage, and no primary source found puts a dollar cost on it, so no money figure appears in the prose.

That the seven algorithms shipped specifically in 4.3BSD Tahoe. The paper read here says only 'we have put seven new algorithms into the 4BSD TCP' and does not name a release, so the prose does not name one either.

The exact dates and durations of the repeat collapses across ARPANET/NSFNET through 1986-87. The paper says only 'the first of what became a series of congestion collapses' and references 'last April's collapse' without a full list.

That the two IMPs on the LBL-to-UC-Berkeley path were specifically ARPANET nodes. Jacobson & Karels say only 'two IMP hops' and name no network; RFC 896 speaks of 'ARPANET IMP based networks' in general. The card now carries only the term-of-art definition of an IMP, not a claim about those two switches.
